---
title: Project scripts
---

A course repository accumulates assumptions: every figure should exist, every
download button should point to a file, every exercise should appear in the
release calendar, and specialist files should still open in the software used
for teaching. Small project-specific scripts can check these assumptions in a
repeatable way.

These checks are especially useful:

- Before a course starts again after several months of inactivity.
- After moving, renaming, or deleting content.
- After changing Quarto configuration, extensions, or dependencies.
- Before publishing a substantial update.
- While diagnosing a failed render or a problem reported by a learner.

The [`structural_biology` validation scripts](https://github.com/au-mbg/structural_biology/tree/main/scripts)
are one worked example. They reflect that repository's layout and teaching
tools; another course should automate its own recurring mistakes rather than
copy every check unchanged.

For related setup, see [Pixi configuration](pixi-configuration.qmd),
[Quarto configuration](quarto-configuration.qmd), and
[Release scheduling](scheduling.qmd).

## What the example project checks

The structure biology project separates checks by responsibility:

| Check | What it catches | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Figures | Missing images and unsupported image formats | Errors fail the check; unused figures are reported as warnings |
| Downloads | Download buttons that refer to missing files | Broken links fail; unreferenced files are reported |
| Quarto navigation | Explicit pages or generated navigation targets that match no `.qmd` files | Invalid targets fail; unreferenced source pages are reported |
| Release schedules | Missing source files and exercises absent from either release calendar | Incomplete or invalid calendars fail |
| PyMOL files | `.pml` scripts or `.pse` sessions that PyMOL cannot load successfully | Invalid files fail |

The checks answer questions specific to the project. For example, its schedule
checker knows that every exercise must occur in both the student and solution
calendars. That rule would be wrong for a repository without scheduled
solutions.

The PyMOL checker is also different from an ordinary file-reference check: it
launches PyMOL in command-line mode and therefore requires PyMOL to be
installed. It searches the system path, supports a `PYMOL_BIN` override, and
also checks the standard macOS application location. A project check should
report external requirements this clearly rather than failing with an obscure
subprocess error.

## Write a small checker

A checker does not need a testing framework or a large abstraction. A useful
starting pattern is:

```python
from pathlib import Path
import sys


REPOSITORY_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CONTENT_ROOT = REPOSITORY_ROOT / "course_notes"
EXCLUDED_DIRECTORIES = {"_site", "_preview", ".quarto"}


def source_documents() -> list[Path]:
    return [
        path
        for path in CONTENT_ROOT.rglob("*.qmd")
        if not EXCLUDED_DIRECTORIES.intersection(path.parts)
    ]


def check_project() -> list[str]:
    problems: list[str] = []

    for document in source_documents():
        if not document.read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip():
            problems.append(f"Empty source document: {document}")

    return problems


def main() -> int:
    problems = check_project()
    for problem in problems:
        print(f"ERROR: {problem}")

    if problems:
        print(f"Found {len(problems)} problem(s).")
        return 1

    print("Check passed.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

This deliberately simple example checks for empty source documents. Replace
that rule with something useful for the course, such as resolving image paths,
comparing schedule entries with exercise files, or validating required front
matter.

Several details make the pattern reliable:

- Resolve the repository relative to `__file__`, rather than assuming the
  command is launched from a particular directory.
- Exclude rendered output and caches from source-file searches.
- Collect all problems so one run gives the maintainer a useful work list.
- Print paths and messages that identify how to fix each problem.
- Exit with `0` when the check passes and a nonzero status when it fails.

The exit status is what lets Pixi, a shell script, or GitHub Actions stop on a
real error. Informational findings such as unused files may instead be warnings
when they do not make the project invalid.

::: {.callout-tip title="Start with recurring mistakes"}
Do not begin by building a general validation framework. When the same mistake
has caused trouble more than once, encode that project rule in the smallest
script that can check it deterministically.
:::

## Expose checks as Pixi tasks

Put validation scripts in a predictable directory such as `scripts/`, then
give contributors stable commands in `pixi.toml`:

```toml
[tasks.check-figures]
cmd = "python scripts/check_figures.py"
description = "Check figure references and report unused figures"

[tasks.check-downloads]
cmd = "python scripts/check_downloads.py"
description = "Check download links and report unreferenced files"

[tasks.check-pymol-scripts]
cmd = "python scripts/check_scripts.py --directory course_notes/files"
description = "Open the course's downloadable PyMOL files"
```

Pixi supplies the Python environment and any declared libraries, so
maintainers do not need to remember which environment or command to use. It
also gives the check a memorable name:

```bash
pixi run check-figures
pixi run check-downloads
pixi run check-pymol-scripts
```

Programs outside the Pixi environment still need to be installed separately.
For example, the structure biology PyMOL checker uses the locally installed
PyMOL executable even though Python runs inside Pixi.

### Check one file while editing

A focused task is convenient when working on one specialist file. Pixi can
declare and forward an argument:

```toml
[tasks.check-script]
cmd = "python scripts/check_scripts.py --file $INIT_CWD/{{file}}"
args = [{ "arg" = "file" }]
description = "Check one PyMOL script"
```

Run it from anywhere in the repository with:

```bash
pixi run check-script course_notes/files/example.pml
```

`$INIT_CWD` is the directory from which the user invoked Pixi. It prevents a
relative file argument from changing meaning if the task itself has a
different working directory.

## Provide one command for routine maintenance

Individual commands are best for fixing one category of problem. Before a new
course run or a large publication, maintainers benefit from one command:

```bash
pixi run check-all
```

In `structural_biology`, `scripts/check_all.py` runs each checker as a separate
subprocess. It records the exit status, continues when one check fails, prints
a final pass/fail table, and exits nonzero if any check failed. The summary
also names the individual Pixi task to rerun for detailed output.

This pattern gives a complete overview without mixing all validation logic
into one program. A new check can be added as another entry in the aggregate
runner while remaining independently usable.

Keep the routine aggregate command reasonably fast. The structure biology
runner checks text-based `.pml` files but skips slower `.pse` session files;
maintainers can run the broader specialist check separately when needed. The
right boundary depends on the course: a check that routinely takes too long is
likely to be skipped.

```toml
[tasks.check-all]
cmd = "python scripts/check_all.py"
description = "Run all local project checks and summarize the results"
```

## Optionally run checks in GitHub Actions

Local use is the first priority: maintainers should be able to run checks
before pushing and see actionable output immediately. Once `check-all` is
stable and non-interactive, the same command can be added to an existing
GitHub Actions build:

```yaml
- name: Run project checks
  run: pixi run check-all
```

Only include checks whose dependencies are available on the Actions runner.
A local check that needs a licensed application, graphical session, or large
download may be better documented as a pre-publication maintainer step. If a
check is required in CI, its nonzero exit status should fail the job.

## Decide what belongs in a script

Good validation targets are deterministic repository properties:

- A referenced local file exists.
- A source page is included in navigation or intentionally excluded.
- Every exercise has a release-calendar entry.
- Required metadata is present and uses an allowed value.
- A domain-specific file can be parsed or opened by its teaching software.

Checks are less suitable for subjective quality such as whether an explanation
is clear, whether a figure is legible, or whether a page looks good on a phone.
Those still require review.

Project checks complement rather than replace:

- A complete Quarto render of every published profile.
- Visual inspection of important pages and generated formats.
- Tests for extension or application code.
- A final review of dates, links, and teaching content.

See [Editing tutorial](../authoring/editing-tutorial.qmd) for the ordinary
edit–preview–render workflow.

## Add checks to another course

1. List mistakes that have previously broken publication or teaching.
2. Choose one rule that can be checked deterministically.
3. Write a small script that reports all violations and returns a meaningful
   exit status.
4. Test it against both valid input and a deliberately broken example.
5. Add an individual Pixi task with a clear name and description.
6. Add fast, reliable checks to `check-all`.
7. Document external requirements and when slower checks should be run.
8. Run the checks before a new course instance and after structural updates.

Keep scripts beside the project rules they enforce and update them when the
repository layout or teaching workflow changes. A stale validator can be as
misleading as having no validator at all.
